sub_answers.sub_question: What are known robustness and generalization limits of neural detectors when deployed under distribution shift or unseen impulsive interference?
sub_answers.text:
Neural or AMP-based detectors achieve optimality only under specific assumptions on the system matrix and constellation, and performance can degrade when those assumptions are violated [d47196s0p0].
Receivers designed for impulsive-noise environments can drastically outperform existing receivers yet still rely on model structure to approach the matched-filter bound, implying limited generalization to unseen interference types that break that structure [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do sample complexity and identifiability bounds constrain learning unknown noise models in MIMO detection?
sub_answers.text:
Blind super-resolution and blind-identification problems are intrinsically ill-posed unless the unknown inputs are constrained to known low-dimensional subspaces, which provides identifiability and enables exact recovery via convex programs [d58777s0p0].
Large-system analyses using state-evolution provide exact analytical characterizations that inform sample-complexity-like regimes where AMP-based detectors attain individually optimal performance in the limit of large dimensions [d47196s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What adversarial, stability, or safety concerns arise when ML detectors operate in safety-critical or regulated communication systems?
sub_answers.text:
Very strong impulsive interference that is much stronger than thermal noise can overwhelm receivers and alter detection performance, posing safety and stability concerns in critical links [d19014s0p0].
Imperfect channel state information and estimation errors are a key stability risk because robustness techniques such as rate-splitting rely on partially decoding interference and on CSI quality to maintain performance [d58875s0p0].
Code-aided joint channel estimation methods are used to refine CSI to mitigate such risks, indicating that detection safety depends on integrating robust estimation into the detector pipeline [d90654s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What open theoretical lower bounds exist on detection error or capacity loss in presence of impulsive noise for data-driven versus model-based detectors?
sub_answers.text:
Theoretical analyses yield optimality conditions and performance limits for large MIMO detection that serve as lower bounds on achievable error rates under the stated assumptions [d47196s0p0].
Practical receivers in impulsive-noise channels can approach the matched-filter bound within about 1 dB, providing an empirical benchmark for capacity-loss or error-gap comparisons between data-driven and model-based detectors [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does improved impulsive-noise handling affect throughput, bit-error rate, and latency in wireless communication systems?
sub_answers.text:
Handling impulsive noise jointly with channel and symbol estimation can drastically reduce bit-error rate and approach the matched-filter bound within about 1 dB in OFDM systems [d19014s0p0].
Mitigating impulsive noise via robust adaptive filtering improves convergence and steady-state error performance under impulse disturbances [d38686s0p0].
A factor-graph-based receiver for impulsive-noise environments can be implemented with O(N log N) complexity and parallelized, which supports higher throughput and lower processing latency in practical implementations [d19014s0p0].
Reduced computational effort of impulsive-noise–robust algorithms lowers processing load and can translate to lower energy per bit in receivers [d38686s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are computational complexity, power, and latency requirements of ML-based detectors compared with classical algorithms in real-time MIMO receivers?
sub_answers.text:
Maximum-likelihood detection achieves high performance but its complexity grows exponentially with spectral efficiency, implying much higher computational cost than classical linear detectors [d140430s0p0].
Specialized near-ML lattice and parallelizable detectors can achieve near-optimal soft-output performance while managing complexity for practical implementations [d140430s0p0].
Iterative Bayesian/AMP-based algorithms can reach optimal performance in large MIMO with low per-iteration complexity and analytically tractable performance/complexity trade-offs, enabling feasible real-time operation [d47196s0p0].
Residual-based and other iterative linear algorithms can cut computational complexity dramatically (for example, one residual-based algorithm reduced complexity by about 87% relative to traditional methods) and thus reduce power consumption and latency in hardware realizations [d42417s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How have learning-based detectors been validated in practical settings such as cellular, Wi-Fi, or radar systems?
sub_answers.text:
Receivers designed for impulsive-noise OFDM environments have been validated with numerical results showing drastic performance improvements over existing receivers and close approach to theoretical bounds [d19014s0p0].
Adaptive filtering methods under the maximum correntropy criterion have been validated via exhaustive simulation studies using correlated inputs and show superior performance in impulsive noise [d38686s0p0].
MIMO techniques for challenging channels, such as underwater optical links, have been validated through analytical BER expressions and photon-counting simulations that confirm performance benefits and extended range under turbulence [d28843s0p0].
Algorithmic validations for MIMO detection approaches include simulation-based comparisons showing substantial BER gains over linear MMSE and alternative methods [d80305s0p0][d140430s0p0].

sub_answers.text: Impulsive noise consists of sporadic, strong interference events that are much stronger than thermal noise and occur in many modern wireless and wireline systems [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What classes of learning-based detectors (e.g., neural nets, deep learning, hybrid models) are used in MIMO detection?
sub_answers.text: Deep learning and neural-network-based data-driven approaches are used for MIMO tasks such as precoding and other signal-processing functions [d71672s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are commonly cited empirical benefits of ML-based detectors versus classical detectors under non-Gaussian noise?
sub_answers.text: ML-based designs can achieve significantly better error performance than classical schemes in some MIMO-OFDM configurations [d29615s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What benchmark datasets and simulation scenarios are used to evaluate detector performance under impulsive noise?
sub_answers.text: Evaluations commonly use computer simulations of MIMO-OFDM systems and OFDM transmissions in impulsive-noise environments, including Wi-Fi and powerline communication scenarios [d29615s0p0][d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do robust loss functions and heavy-tailed likelihood models (e.g., alpha-stable, mixture models) represent impulsive noise?
sub_answers.text: Robust loss functions represent impulsive or heavy-tailed noise by replacing mean-squared-error with a kernel-based estimate of the residual density that maximizes an estimated log-likelihood, which coincides with MSE under Gaussian errors but remains stable under heavy-tailed noise [d115559s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What architectures and training strategies (e.g., model-based deep unfolding, autoencoders, RNNs) are used for MIMO detection?
sub_answers.text: Data-driven neural detectors use deep networks with ReLU activations to learn detection mappings and can asymptotically approach the MAP detector given sufficient training data [d67352s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do parameter estimation methods (e.g., EM, variational inference, robust estimation) learn unknown noise distributions from data?
sub_answers.text: Loopy belief propagation methods combine GAMP with forward-backward algorithms and turbo decoding to jointly estimate latent parameters including noise impulses and channel coefficients [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do feature representations and input preprocessing (e.g., pilot-based estimation, denoising) enable detectors to separate signal from impulsive disturbances?
sub_answers.text: Joint estimation frameworks explicitly estimate channel coefficients, noise impulses, and symbols together, allowing the detector to separate signal and impulsive disturbances within a factor-graph inference process [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What theoretical results exist on universal approximation or consistency of neural detectors under model mismatch or heavy-tailed noise?
sub_answers.text: Data-driven deep detectors can asymptotically approach the MAP detector under broad scenarios, given sufficiently many training samples [d67352s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What empirical and theoretical studies characterize how neural-network based signal detectors degrade when channel statistics change (covariate shift, nonstationarity) or when exposed to rare, high-amplitude impulsive interference (alpha-stable noise, Middleton models)?
sub_answers.text:
Neural-network based algorithms for interference whitening can be trained to select covariance-computation options across diverse interference scenarios and can minimize BLER under both trained and untrained interference conditions [d77545s0p0].
Receivers that jointly estimate channel, noise impulses, symbols, and bits using factor-graph methods with GAMP are near-optimal in impulsive-noise OFDM and can drastically outperform existing receivers, coming within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound in simulations [d19014s0p0].
Generator-guided samplers that model jump components explicitly provide robust estimation for OFDM-SISO channel estimation under mixed Gaussian and impulsive noise, offering a tradeoff between complexity and performance when jump structure is accounted for [d128145s0p0].
Message-passing detectors suffer performance degradation under highly correlated or ill-conditioned MIMO channels, and EP-based partitioning methods mitigate but do not eliminate those degradation mechanisms [d113968s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are provable sample complexity rates, parameter identifiability conditions, and convergence guarantees for algorithms that jointly estimate MIMO channel and unknown impulsive/noise-corruption models (e.g., mixture, heavy-tailed, or sparse interference) from finite training data?
sub_answers.text:
A factor-graph approach that jointly estimates channel and impulsive noise yields a computationally tractable near-optimal receiver with O(N log N) complexity for N tones, but no explicit provable sample-complexity rates or identifiability conditions are provided in that treatment [d19014s0p0].
Generator-guided inverse-sampling methods for L\'evy-driven models derive structured reverse samplers that amortize large-jump rates with neural networks to improve tractability, but no finite-sample convergence guarantees or parameter-identifiability theorems are stated in that work [d128145s0p0].
Supervised learning for covariance selection reduces whitening complexity and minimizes BLER across scenarios, but explicit sample-complexity bounds or convergence proofs for joint channel-and-noise estimation are not reported in that study [d77545s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which documented failure modes, certified-robustness limits, or regulatory compliance risks (e.g., fault tolerance, false alarm/missed-detection bounds) have been reported for ML-based detectors deployed in safety-critical or regulated communication contexts (aviation, medical telemetry, industrial control), and what mitigation audits or verification methods exist?
sub_answers.text:
Machine-learning selection of interference-whitening options can reduce computation from O(N^3) to O(N) by approximating the covariance as diagonal when spatial correlation is low, thereby affecting fault-tolerance tradeoffs through algorithmic simplification [d77545s0p0].
Joint factor-graph receivers that explicitly estimate impulses and channels achieve near-optimal BER performance in impulsive-noise OFDM, indicating practical robustness but no certified-robustness bounds or regulatory-compliance risk analyses are provided [d19014s0p0].
EP-based detectors for highly correlated MIMO explicitly address degradation modes due to channel ill-conditioning but do not provide documented certified-robustness limits or formal fault-tolerance guarantees in regulated contexts [d113968s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What formal lower bounds or impossibility results compare minimax detection error, achievable rate/capacity loss, or required SNR under impulsive/noisy channels for data-driven (learning-based) detectors versus classical model-based detectors, including assumptions on noise tails (alpha-stable, Middleton classes) and channel uncertainty?
sub_answers.text:
A factor-graph based joint estimator for OFDM in impulsive noise achieves performance within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound in simulations, implying small gaps to optimality in studied settings but not formal lower-bound or impossibility theorems comparing learning-based and model-based detectors [d19014s0p0].
Generator-guided analysis of L\'evy-driven dynamics shows that reversed jump components become state-dependent and motivates samplers that decompose diffusion, small jumps, and large jumps, but does not present formal minimax lower bounds or capacity-loss comparisons under heavy-tailed noise classes [d128145s0p0].
No formal impossibility results or SNR requirement lower bounds for data-driven detectors versus classical model-based detectors under alpha-stable or Middleton noise classes are reported in the cited works [d128145s0p0][d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Quantitatively, how does robust mitigation of impulsive noise (e.g., alpha-stable, Middleton, bursty interference) change achievable throughput (Mbps), packet error rate / BER, and end-to-end air-interface latency in specific wireless links (LTE/5G NR, 802.11ax/ay, V2X) under measured interference profiles?
sub_answers.text:
A factor-graph-based OFDM receiver for impulsive noise environments drastically outperforms existing receivers and operates within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound in BER performance [d19014s0p0].
The same receiver jointly estimates channel coefficients, noise impulses, symbols, and bits to achieve that performance under impulsive interference models [d19014s0p0].
The receiver scales with O(N log N) complexity for N tones and is parallelizable, which impacts real-time throughput and latency budgets by enabling efficient implementation [d19014s0p0].
Machine-learning-based spatial interference-whitening can select covariance-computation options to minimize BLER across interference regimes and reduce whitening complexity when spatial correlation is low, affecting achievable link reliability and throughput under interference-dominant versus noise-dominant scenarios [d77545s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: For real-time MIMO receivers, what are the measured algorithmic complexity (FLOPs or MACs per symbol), memory footprint, energy consumption (mJ/op or mW at target clock), and processing latency (µs/frame) of representative ML-based detectors (NNs, CNNs, RNNs, transformers, unfolded algorithms) compared to classical methods (ZF, MMSE, sphere decoding, message passing) on common hardware targets (ARM Cortex-M, DSPs, GPUs, FPGAs, ASICs)?
sub_answers.text:
Approximating the interference-plus-noise covariance as diagonal reduces whitening complexity from O(N^3) to O(N) when spatial correlation is low, lowering per-frame computational cost for MIMO receivers [d77545s0p0].
A factor-graph receiver that merges GAMP with forward–backward and turbo decoding achieves overall receiver complexity of O(N log N) for N OFDM tones, enabling tractable joint estimation in impulsive noise scenarios [d19014s0p0].
Iterative PMSE-based precoding/decoding algorithms provide near-optimal performance with greatly reduced computational complexity compared to intractable PDetMSE minimization, lowering implementation cost for multiuser MIMO systems [d4001s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What empirical evidence exists from field trials, testbeds, or product deployments showing performance of learning-based detection in real-world cellular (e.g., 4G/5G), Wi‑Fi (802.11 variants), or radar/automotive systems — including measured link-level KPIs (BLER, throughput), robustness to channel nonidealities, and integration challenges (synchronization, fading, mobility)?
sub_answers.text:
Link-level evaluations of Rate-Splitting Multiple Access (RSMA) confirm significant throughput benefits over SDMA and NOMA in simulations and link-level tests, showing robustness benefits in multi-antenna downlink scenarios [d58875s0p0].
A supervised learning algorithm for interference-whitening was shown to minimize BLER under both trained and untrained interference scenarios in experimental evaluations, demonstrating practical robustness to diverse interference conditions [d77545s0p0].
MIMO techniques in underwater optical channels are shown in simulation and photon-counting evaluations to mitigate turbulence-induced fading and extend viable communication range, demonstrating empirical BER improvements for MIMO in nonideal channels [d28843s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Define impulsive noise in digital communications, describe common statistical models used to represent it (e.g., alpha-stable, Middleton Class A/B, Bernoulli-Gaussian), and contrast their statistical properties with additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) in terms of tails, variance behavior, moment existence, and impact on detector likelihoods.

Survey the families of learning-based MIMO detectors in the literature: model-driven approaches (e.g., learned iterative algorithms, unfolding of message-passing or approximate MAP solvers), purely data-driven neural networks (e.g., fully connected, CNN, RNN, transformers), hybrid architectures (e.g., neural pre/post-processing paired with classical detectors), and noteworthy variants (e.g., reinforcement learning for scheduling, GANs for channel/impulse modeling).

List empirical performance improvements reported for machine-learning-based MIMO detectors compared to classical detectors under non-Gaussian/impulsive noise, specifying metrics and scenarios (BER/FER reduction, robustness to outliers, SNR gap, computational trade-offs), and cite typical conditions where gains are largest (sparsity of impulses, heavy-tailed noise parameters, imperfect CSI).

Identify standard benchmark datasets, synthetic noise generators, and simulation setups used to evaluate detector performance under impulsive noise: common channel models (Rayleigh/Rician, correlated channels), standard impulsive-noise models and parameter ranges (Middleton Class A, alpha-stable characteristic exponents, Bernoulli-Gaussian impulse probability and amplitude), and publicly available datasets or repositories, plus recommended evaluation protocols (Monte Carlo trials, SNR sweeps, channel estimation error models).

In what mathematical forms do robust loss functions (e.g., Huber, Tukey's bisquare, correntropy) and heavy-tailed probabilistic models (e.g., symmetric alpha-stable laws, Student's t, Gaussian scale mixtures) capture impulsive, spiky interference in communication channels, and how do their tail indices, influence functions, or likelihood shapes quantify impulsiveness?
sub_answers.text:
The Huber loss is used to replace Gaussian likelihoods with a piecewise quadratic-linear likelihood that bounds the influence of large residuals and thus models impulsive outliers via a transition between L2 and L1 behavior [d82363s0p0].
Huber-type estimators implement L1-norm weighting on outliers so that the effective influence function is bounded and robustness holds even when only second moments exist, which quantifies impulsiveness by reducing sensitivity to extreme deviations [d84229s0p0].
Correntropy-based penalties and nonparametric kernel log-likelihoods capture impulsive noise by emphasizing local similarity in residuals and by reshaping the loss to downweight large errors relative to MSE, thereby modifying likelihood shape to tolerate heavy tails [d115559s0p0].
Heavy-tailed probabilistic models such as Student's t, Laplace, and Cauchy are explicitly used to represent thick-tailed additive errors and thus quantify impulsiveness through their tail decay parameters and scale, with Student's t and Cauchy exhibiting heavier tails than Gaussian models [d82363s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which neural and hybrid architectures have been applied to multi-antenna symbol detection—such as model-driven deep unfolding of iterative detectors, learned belief-propagation networks, convolutional/transformer front-ends combined with fully connected decoders, sequence models like LSTMs/GRUs, and autoencoder-based end-to-end transceivers—and what training regimes (losses, curriculum learning, supervised vs. self-supervised, transfer learning) and complexity/latency trade-offs were reported?
sub_answers.text:
Convolutional neural networks and LSTM architectures have been applied to forecasting distributional parameters and therefore to sequence- and feature-based detection problems in communications, using custom negative log-likelihood losses to train distributional outputs [d112650s0p0].
A factor-graph hybrid receiver merges generalized approximate message passing (GAMP) with forward-backward algorithms and soft-input soft-output decoding in a turbo-like architecture to jointly estimate channel, noise impulses, symbols, and bits for OFDM in impulsive environments [d19014s0p0].
Model-driven message-passing approaches implemented via loopy belief propagation achieve near-optimal performance while retaining tractable complexity and parallelizability, with the factor-graph receiver operating at O(N log N) complexity for N tones [d19014s0p0].
Training regimes include direct optimization of distributional negative log-likelihood losses for deep nets, as used for Student's t and skewed Student's t parameter forecasting, enabling supervised likelihood-based training for heavy-tailed targets [d112650s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What algorithms estimate unknown heavy-tailed or non-Gaussian noise parameters from observations—specifically which implementations of Expectation-Maximization, variational Bayes, method-of-moments, robust M-estimators, characteristic-function-based estimators, or score-matching approaches have been used to infer parameters (tail index, scale, mixing weights) for alpha-stable, mixture, or t-distributed noise in communications datasets, and what are their sample-complexity and convergence properties?
sub_answers.text:
Hyperparameters in Gaussian process regression are estimated via type II maximum likelihood (evidence maximization) when robustifying models with alternative likelihoods such as the Huber likelihood [d82363s0p0].
Estimators based on minimizing the Huber loss provide robustness to heavy tails and are consistent even when only the second moment exists, which offers a practical M-estimation approach to infer scale and related parameters under heavy-tailed noise [d84229s0p0].
Sparse Fourier–transform-based algorithms enable learning mixture-model parameters for heavy-tailed components and yield polynomial-time/sample consistent parameter recovery for certain heavy-tailed families, enabling robust mean estimation against noise-oblivious adversaries [d118117s0p0].
Correntropy-induced metric constrained normalized LMP algorithms exploit sparsity and include variable-regularization mechanisms to adapt convergence and steady-state performance when identifying non-Gaussian impulsive-noise systems [d26508s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which input processing and feature-engineering techniques (for example pilot-aided impulse detection, blanking/clipping, rank-reduction projections, wavelet or short-time Fourier preprocessing, higher-order statistics, or learned denoisers) have been used to transform raw MIMO observations so neural or model-based detectors can disentangle transmitted symbols from impulsive bursts, and what performance gains or robustness benchmarks were reported?
sub_answers.text:
Joint estimation on a factor graph can explicitly estimate noise impulses together with channel and symbols, allowing the receiver to disentangle impulsive bursts from transmitted data via message passing [d19014s0p0].
Sparsity-aware adaptive filtering using normalized least-mean-p algorithms with correntropy-induced metric penalties and variable regularization exploits sparse impulse structure to mitigate impulsive noise and improve convergence and steady-state error [d26508s0p0].
Kernel-based residual-density losses and nonparametric likelihood maximization reshape residual treatment so that large noise bursts are downweighted, which improves robustness of downstream detectors to large transient errors [d115559s0p0].
High-dimensional sparse Fourier transforms have been used as a preprocessing/estimation tool to separate heavy-tailed mixture components and support consistent robust mean estimation in the presence of impulsive noise [d118117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What theoretical guarantees have been proved for learned MIMO detectors under misspecified noise—such as universal approximation bounds, consistency of parameter/decision estimators, robustness to heavy tails (e.g., asymptotic error rates, breakdown points), or PAC-style generalization bounds for networks trained under different noise families (Gaussian vs. alpha-stable or mixtures)?
sub_answers.text:
Consistency results have been proved for estimators that minimize the Huber loss, showing robustness to heavy tails and consistency even when only second moments exist [d84229s0p0].
Polynomial-time and sample-consistent algorithms have been established for learning parameters of certain heavy-tailed mixture models using sparse Fourier techniques, including cases without finite covariances [d118117s0p0].
Wasserstein-stability-based generalization bounds and resultant generalization guarantees have been developed for heavy-tailed SGD modeled by heavy-tailed SDEs, yielding bounds that illuminate non-monotonic relationships between tail-heaviness and generalization without strong topological assumptions [d82558s0p0].
Analysis of robust kernel-based losses shows that choosing such losses can remove spurious local minima under restricted isometry conditions and improve robustness across diverse noise distributions, providing optimization-landscape guarantees for robust nonconvex estimation problems [d115559s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Under realistic distribution shift and unexpected bursty/impulsive interference, what empirical and theoretical limits have been reported on the robustness and out-of-distribution generalization of learned neural signal detectors (e.g., NN-based symbol detectors, deep unfolding networks)? Cite concrete failure modes, performance degradation curves, and conditions (SNR ranges, impulse rates, non-Gaussian tail indices) where these models break down.
sub_answers.text: CLIP-based and CNN-based forensic detectors are both vulnerable to white-box adversarial attacks that cause severe performance degradation under crafted perturbations [d98719s0p0].

sub_answers.text: A factor-graph-based receiver for OFDM in impulsive noise environments drastically outperforms existing receivers on BER/FER metrics and approaches within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound under the studied impulsive-noise conditions [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Survey how learning-based MIMO detectors have been validated outside simulations: list over-the-air experiments, testbed results, and commercial or standardization trials in cellular (LTE, 5G NR), Wi‑Fi (802.11ac/ax/be), and radar (automotive, FMCW) systems; report the evaluation setups, measured gains or degradations versus baselines, datasets used, and reproducibility (open datasets/code).

sub_answers.sub_question: Specify practical training-data and pilot design requirements for deploying ML detectors in operational MIMO links: typical dataset sizes and diversity (hours of IQ captures, number of channels/power/SNRs), labeling strategies (supervised with transmitted symbols, unsupervised/self-supervised, synthetic augmentation), required channel/pilot patterns and pilot overhead, acceptable mismatch tolerance (how much channel nonstationarity/DRIFT is tolerated), and guidance on online adaptation frequency and transfer learning to new deployment sites.

sub_answers.sub_question: Describe the architecture and operational principles of MIMO wireless systems (e.g., spatial multiplexing, diversity, beamforming) and enumerate the main signal-processing tasks and difficulties they introduce (channel estimation, detection/decoding complexity, interference mitigation, synchronization).
sub_answers.text: MIMO techniques allow for spatial multiplexing and/or diversity gain in wireless systems [d5873s0p0]. Multiple antennas provide extra dimensions of channel estimation data and can yield a security gain over SISO systems [d5873s0p0]. Channel estimation is a key signal-processing task exploited in MIMO systems for functions such as authentication and detection [d5873s0p0]. Maximum-likelihood detection complexity grows exponentially with spectral efficiency, motivating list and lattice decoding approaches to reduce complexity [d140430s0p0]. Sphere decoders and similar ML-oriented algorithms suffer high computational complexity at low-to-moderate SNRs, prompting sequential decoding and time-out strategies to reduce complexity while preserving performance tradeoffs [d10162s0p0]. Hybrid precoding and joint channel estimation and detection techniques are used to mitigate inter-user interference in multiuser MIMO systems [d111619s0p0].

Rayleigh, EPA/ETU taps, and any publicly available recorded impulsive-noise datasets or repositories used in prior work).

How do robust loss formulations (e.g., Huber, Tukey's biweight, correntropy) and explicit heavy-tailed likelihood families (alpha-stable distributions, symmetric/compound Poisson impulsive models, Gaussian scale mixtures) mathematically model impulsive spike noise; what are their tails, influence functions, and resulting MAP/ML estimators in signal recovery tasks?
sub_answers.text: The Huber likelihood replaces quadratic penalty with a piecewise loss that is L1-weighted on large residuals to bound the influence of outliers and provide robustness to heavy tails in Gaussian process regression and tensor factor models [d82363s0p0][d84229s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which neural and hybrid architectures have been proposed for multi-antenna (MIMO) symbol detection — including model-based deep unfolding of iterative algorithms (e.g., unfolded message passing, approximate message passing), detector-specific autoencoder designs, recurrent architectures (LSTM/GRU) processing sequential MIMO streams, and graph neural networks on factor graphs — and what training regimes (supervised, self-supervised, curriculum, transfer learning) and loss functions yield best bit-error-rate/complexity trade-offs?
sub_answers.text: A factor-graph receiver merges generalized approximate message passing (GAMP) with forward–backward message passing and turbo decoding to jointly estimate channel, noise impulses, symbols, and bits in OFDM under impulsive noise [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which parameter-learning procedures (classical EM for mixture/GSM/alpha-stable approximations, stochastic variational inference for nonconjugate heavy-tailed priors, M-estimators and robustified moment methods, and Bayesian hierarchical learning with empirical Bayes) have been used to infer unknown impulsive-noise parameters from received wireless data, what convergence guarantees or regularization choices are recommended, and how are hyperparameters initialized in practice?
sub_answers.text: Hyperparameters of Gaussian process models are learned by maximizing the model evidence (type II maximum likelihood) for regression under robust likelihoods [d82363s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What input-feature constructions and preprocessing pipelines (pilot-aided channel and impulse-noise estimation, time-frequency denoising using median/alpha-trim filters, wavelet-based spike removal, robust covariance estimation, and learned front-ends such as convolutional denoisers or denoising autoencoders) have been shown to improve detection under impulsive disturbances, and how are pilot design, windowing, and feature normalization tailored to preserve symbol information while suppressing impulses?
sub_answers.text: Joint estimation receivers perform simultaneous channel and impulse-noise estimation along with symbol decoding on OFDM tones, enabling pilot and data information to be fused in a single inference process [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What provable results address the statistical consistency, robustness, or universal approximation properties of neural detectors under model mismatch or heavy-tailed noise — for example, bounds on excess risk for networks trained with robust losses, asymptotic consistency of learned detectors when true noise is alpha-stable or mixture-type, and guarantees for generalization of unfolded algorithms or networks under heavy-tailed observation models?
sub_answers.text: Estimators minimizing the Huber loss yield robustness to heavy tails and consistency of factor estimates even when only the second moment of the data exists in tensor-factor models [d84229s0p0].
